transcript: What are some of the best musicals of all time from a book perspective? I am gonna answer this question for myself, and of course, I wanna hear everyone else's opinions, too. But as usual, I'm gonna come at this from a few different angles. I think first you absolutely have to talk about some of these big, famous classic musicals, like cabaret, A Chorus Line, Gypsy, Hello, Dolly, how to succeed in business without really trying, and maybe most of all, Fiddler on the roof. There’s a lot more musicals I'm gonna talk about in this video, but just to kinda spoil it, I think there's a real case to be made that Fiddler on the roof is maybe the best musical theatre book of all time. Then I think a lot of Sondheim's most famous musicals have really extraordinary books, too. I mean, into the Woods, Sweeney Todd, A Little Night Music Company, Follies. You might notice there's a big one missing from that list, but I'm gonna talk about it in a minute. All of these really famous classics are classics for a reason. They've stood the test of time for a reason. And I think no small part of that is the really solid foundation of the book. You also absolutely have to talk about Oscar Hammerstein II, where, even though his writing definitely shows its age in a variety of ways, his work remains really brilliant in more ways than not. And it was pushing a lot of boundaries. As far as some other old school classics that I personally really love the books for, I would say Annie, 1776 and the fantasticks. But what about more contemporary shows? Well, I would say some of the best and most well constructed musical books in the last 30 years or so include Caroline or Change, Fun Home, next to normal. I know some people find in the Heights to be a little juvenile, but I think it's a really great book. Matilda Ragtime Parade. Of the really recent shows, I think Maybe Happy Ending probably has the best book we've seen in a while. And yes, a lot of those skew more dramatic and emotional, and maybe that's my preference, but I also think there are some great contemporary comedic books. Urintetown, Bat Boy, Avenue Q, Spelling Bee. Another sort of “category” of book I wanna talk about are the ones that are, like, pretty closely adapted from, like, a movie or something. And a lot of people will be quick to criticize these and be like, “well, they just copied the screenplay of the movie.” And, like, yes, I agree with that to some extent, and I think probably I do have more respect at the end of the day for something that is doing a lot more heavy lifting from an adaptation standpoint. But in a landscape where *so many* of these musicals are just taking a movie, plopping it on stage and stuffing some songs into it. There's something to be said for the people who actually did that, and it was really good. I think examples of that include The Band's Visit, Billy Elliot, once, a man of no importance. But the last “category,” I guess, that I wanna talk about is kind of the reverse of that: musicals that are either very original or take big swings with the adaptation. I'm thinking about rent, Hadestown, Scottsboro Boys, a lot of Dave Malloy's work, and, of course, my favorite musical of all time, Sunday in the park with George. And yeah, some of the musicals I just named have books that are maybe more flawed than the ones in the rest of the video. But because of their ambitions and their intelligence and their creativity and their depth of feeling, I think the overall net achievement that they're able to reach is sometimes greater than some of these traditionally well constructed ones. But the very last point I'm gonna make is that if you look at this list, a lot of it is mostly just like…my favorite musicals, which gets to the heart of this issue. If you're talking about the merits of a musical and you're not considering its book, you're doing it wrong.
